A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison after matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: V1 reports original five-domain LLM evaluations, IdeaMatcher comparisons, human ratings of 460 generated ideas, and supplementary analyses of background knowledge, input content, and errors.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds Physics human evaluations and results for newer language models.

M1.justification: The generation prompts now request explicit paper understanding, consideration of related work, and step-by-step reasoning; the main prompt also explicitly requests ideas distinct from related papers. The distinctness encoder changes from bert-base-uncased to text-embedding-ada-002. These are limited procedural and component changes within the retained generation, matching, and retrieval framework.

E1.justification: The original five domains remain. Appendix K adds a separate Computer Science cohort published in January–March 2025, extending the original 2023–2024 temporal coverage. Human novelty, relevance, and feasibility assessment also extends from Computer Science to Physics, which already had automated evaluation.

E2.justification: V2 adds an evaluated Computer Science comparison containing GPT-4o, Claude-3, Gemini-2.5, and Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct alongside Claude-2, Gemini-1.0, and GPT-4 (Figure 7; Appendices J–K). The original four-model benchmark and RoBERTa/BERTScore/GPT IdeaMatcher comparison remain. Correcting GPT-3 labels to GPT-3.5 does not introduce another comparator.

E3.justification: The reported main sample increases from 100 to 250 papers per domain, and Computer Science human evaluation changes from 460 ideas across 46 papers to 660 across 66. V2 adds Physics evaluation of 630 ideas across 63 papers and a 200-paper protocol for newer models. The distinctness embedding also changes. These are substantial reported setting changes, although the PDFs do not establish which retained results were recomputed.

E4.justification: Appendix G adds an infeasible-idea case involving inaccessible private peer-review discussions, extending the existing generic-idea and author-omission error analysis. The title/abstract comparison, idea-length analysis, background-knowledge experiment, and memorization checks remain substantially unchanged.

E5.justification: Both versions report double annotation of 20% of human-evaluated ideas, Cohen's kappa of 0.83 for idea evaluation, and 0.94 for dataset annotation. Neither adds generation-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance testing. Increased evaluation sample sizes change E3, not the uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: V2 adds Physics novelty, relevance, and feasibility results, including GPT-4 relevance of 91.56% and feasibility of 94.78%. Figure 7 newly reports IAScores around 0.41 for GPT-4o, 0.39 for Claude-3, 0.37 for Gemini-2.5, and 0.31 for Llama-70B. These extend the result set substantially. Existing Computer Science human percentages remain unchanged; the new cohort prevents treating the added scores as established same-setting improvements.

T1.justification: V2 Section 4.3 introduces author-defined and valid-idea sets, assumes the former is a subset of the latter, and decomposes the probability of generating a valid idea to motivate a lower-bound interpretation of IAScore. This is a limited addition to formal reasoning; the original metric equations (1)–(4) remain.

C1.justification: V2 adds explicit claims that no task-specific automated evaluation metric exists and that IAScore provides a lower-bound indicator of model competence. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion consequently foreground scalable automated evaluation as the central contribution. The earlier claims about model rankings and LLM idea-generation capability remain elsewhere in the paper.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's recognition that authors may omit useful ideas, new Section 7.3 discusses dependence on reference quality, failure to assess depth or feasibility, and cosine similarity missing meaningful distinctions. Section 4.3 also interprets author alignment as a necessary credibility check. These additions materially expand the metrics' interpretation and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: V2 supplies model identifiers and stated training cutoffs, describes splitting overlength papers and combining generated ideas, and specifies plain-text inputs excluding figures, tables, and references. It also expands annotation-payment and filtering explanations. These are useful disclosures; their addition alone does not establish changed implementation. The public repository remains the same.

R1.justification: V2 shortens the SciMON description and removes the detailed FAQ comparison while retaining the distinction between generating ideas and evaluating LLM capabilities. It adds the OpenAI embedding reference and removes the Devlin and Young references. Consolidating the two Kumar entries concerns the same work, not removal of a separate research contribution.

P1.justification: The abstract is extensively rewritten and the document is substantially reorganized. Generation and background-knowledge procedures move into Experiments; annotation details, human-evaluation questions, and detailed dataset discussion are consolidated in appendices. The FAQ disappears, references precede the appendices, and new limitations and model-evaluation sections reshape the narrative.

P2.justification: V2 combines the separate dataset plots into Figure 2a–b, redraws the alignment chart, updates model labels, and relocates the editing example and retrieval diagram between the main text and appendices. It adds the newer-model chart and summary Tables 7–8 and rearranges the feedback-form pages. This substantially changes visual organization while retaining most original plotted content.

improvement.justification: Physics ratings, newer-model results, implementation disclosures, and explicit metric limitations improve breadth and transparency. However, v2 retains the Computer Science percentages and distinctness plot despite changing their reported sample size and encoder, without reconciling those changes. Figure 7 does not clearly establish a common evaluation cohort for old and new models. The new probability decomposition also does not establish the claimed lower bound for the author-normalized IAScore. These issues affect the newly emphasized central contribution, preventing a reliable net-quality judgment.
